findings.title: GPUStack: Authentication bypass via trusted loopback source (reverse-proxy TCP peer or X-GPUStack-Real-IP header) grants unauthenticated admin
findings.summary:
### Impact

In GPUStack before v2.2.0, `get_current_user` (in `gpustack/api/auth.py`) promotes any request whose source is considered loopback to the built-in administrator account when `force_auth_localhost` is `False` (the default). The "source" is derived by `client_ip_getter`, which can be made to report `127.0.0.1` without any credentials in two ways:

1. **Same-host reverse proxy (TCP peer).** In the canonical self-hosted shape —
   GPUStack behind a same-host reverse proxy with `proxy_pass
   http://127.0.0.1:<port>` — every remote request arrives at GPUStack with TCP
   peer `127.0.0.1`, so the loopback auto-admin branch fires. No header or
   credential is required. Verified end-to-end against HEAD `6bee5883`.
2. **`X-GPUStack-Real-IP` header.** A forged `X-GPUStack-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1`
   header can cause the request source to be treated as loopback.

Either path yields **full, unauthenticated administrative access** over the network: enumerate and modify users, models, workers, and configuration; mint persistent admin API keys (scope `["*"]`, valid from any source IP thereafter); read worker credentials and cloud/provider secrets. Combined with admin-only functionality such as `POST /v2/inference-backends/from yaml`, this leads to code execution on worker hosts.

This vulnerability has been observed exploited in the wild against a v2.1.1 deployment (attacker-created custom backends running reverse shells).

### Root cause

Trusting the network source of a request (socket peer, or a client-controllable header) as an authentication signal. When GPUStack is fronted by a same-host reverse proxy, the socket peer is always loopback, so the "localhost is trusted" assumption no longer holds.

### Patches

Fixed in `gpustack` `2.2.0`: the loopback auto-admin path was removed and client-IP / forwarding-header handling was hardened. Upgrade to `2.2.0` or later.

### Workarounds

- Set `force_auth_localhost=true` to require authentication even for loopback
  requests.

findings.title: U.S. urges critical infrastructure orgs to secure refrigeration systems ASAP after EU supermarket and blood bank attacks
findings.summary: Following recent cyber attacks on French blood banks and European supermarkets, U.S. federal agencies are urging critical infrastructure organizations to immediately secure industrial refrigeration systems against remote tampering and temperature manipulation. Key takeaways Cybercriminals are actively targeting unpatched flaws, misconfigurations, and weak or hard-coded passwords in commercial cold-chain and refrigeration controllers globally. Attackers are gaining remote access to manipulate temperature controls and spoil essential products, such as blood and food. CISA, the FBI, and other U.S. agencies are advising organizations to isolate OT systems, secure or remove remote access, patch critical vulnerabilities, and replace end-of-life devices. Critical infrastructure organizations in the healthcare, chemicals, transportation, and food and agriculture sectors must urgently harden their industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems to protect food, medicines, and other essential products against ongoing cyber attacks. That’s the call from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and other U.S. government agencies, following a series of alarming breaches against refrigeration systems in French blood banks and European supermarkets . “Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” CISA Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera said in a statement. Attackers are remotely targeting electronic-temperature and commercial-refrigeration controllers used in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. They’re looking for unpatched vulnerabilities and other security flaws, such as misconfigurations, according to the agencies. Once attackers gain remote access to these systems, they try to tamper with these machines’ temperature controls to damage their refrigerated products. findings.title: AI threats in the wild: The current state of prompt injections on the web
findings.summary: Posted by Thomas Brunner, Yu-Han Liu, Moni Pande At Google, our Threat Intelligence teams are dedicated to staying ahead of real-world adversarial activity, proactively monitoring emerging threats before they can impact users. Right now, Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) is a top priority for the security community, anticipating it as a primary attack vector for adversaries to target and compromise AI agents. But while the danger of IPI is widely discussed, are threat actors actually exploiting this vector today – and if so, how? To answer these questions and to uncover real-world abuse, we initiated a broad sweep of the public web to monitor for known indirect prompt injection patterns. This is what we found. The threat of indirect prompt injection Unlike a direct injection where a user "jailbreaks" a chatbot, IPI occurs when an AI system processes content—like a website, email, or document—that contains malicious instructions. When the AI reads this poisoned content, it may silently follow the attacker's commands instead of the user's original intent. This is not a new area of concern for us and Google has been working tirelessly to combat these threats. Our efforts involve cross-functional collaboration between researchers at Google DeepMind (GDM) and defenders like the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG). We have previously detailed our work in this area and researchers have further highlighted the evolving nature of these vulnerabilities. Despite this collective focus, a fundamental question remains: to what degree are real-world malicious actors currently operationalizing these attacks? Proactive monitoring at Google The landscape of IPI on the web There are many channels through which attackers might try to send prompt injections. findings.title: Google Workspace’s continuous approach to mitigating indirect prompt injections
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team Indirect prompt injection (IPI) is an evolving threat vector targeting users of complex AI applications with multiple data sources, such as Workspace with Gemini. This technique enables the attacker to influence the behavior of an LLM by injecting malicious instructions into the data or tools used by the LLM as it completes the user’s query. This may even be possible without any input directly from the user. IPI is not the kind of technical problem you “solve” and move on. Sophisticated LLMs with increasing use of agentic automation combined with a wide range of content create an ultra-dynamic and evolving playground for adversarial attacks. That’s why Google takes a sophisticated and comprehensive approach to these attacks. We’re continuously improving LLM resistance to IPI attacks and launching AI application capabilities with ever-improving defenses. Staying ahead of the latest indirect prompt injection attacks is critical to our mission of securing Workspace with Gemini. In our previous blog “ Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy ”, we reviewed the layered architecture of our IPI defenses. In this blog, we’ll share more detail on the continuous approach we take to improve these defenses and to solve for new attacks. findings.title: Architecting Security for Agentic Capabilities in Chrome
findings.summary: Posted by Nathan Parker, Chrome security team Chrome has been advancing the web’s security for well over 15 years, and we’re committed to meeting new challenges and opportunities with AI. Billions of people trust Chrome to keep them safe by default, and this is a responsibility we take seriously. Following the recent launch of Gemini in Chrome and the preview of agentic capabilities , we want to share our approach and some new innovations to improve the safety of agentic browsing. The primary new threat facing all agentic browsers is indirect prompt injection . It can appear in malicious sites, third-party content in iframes, or from user-generated content like user reviews, and can cause the agent to take unwanted actions such as initiating financial transactions or exfiltrating sensitive data. Given this open challenge, we are investing in a layered defense that includes both deterministic and probabilistic defenses to make it difficult and costly for attackers to cause harm. Designing safe agentic browsing for Chrome has involved deep collaboration of security experts across Google. We built on Gemini's existing protections and agent security principles and have implemented several new layers for Chrome. We’re introducing a user alignment critic where the agent’s actions are vetted by a separate model that is isolated from untrusted content. We’re also extending Chrome’s origin-isolation capabilities to constrain what origins the agent can interact with, to just those that are relevant to the task. Our layered defense also includes user confirmations for critical steps, real-time detection of threats , and red-teaming and response . We’ll step through these layers below. Checking agent outputs with User Alignment Critic The main planning model for Gemini uses page content shared in Chrome to decide what action to take next. findings.summary: Posted by Jeff Vander Stoep, Android Last year, we wrote about why a memory safety strategy that focuses on vulnerability prevention in new code quickly yields durable and compounding gains. This year we look at how this approach isn’t just fixing things, but helping us move faster . The 2025 data continues to validate the approach, with memory safety vulnerabilities falling below 20% of total vulnerabilities for the first time. Updated data for 2025. This post is published a couple of months before the end of 2025, but Android’s industry-standard 90-day patch window means that these results are very likely close to final. We can and will accelerate patching when necessary. We adopted Rust for its security and are seeing a 1000x reduction in memory safety vulnerability density compared to Android’s C and C++ code . But the biggest surprise was Rust's impact on software delivery. With Rust changes having a 4x lower rollback rate and spending 25% less time in code review , the safer path is now also the faster one. findings.title: Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team With the rapid adoption of generative AI, a new wave of threats is emerging across the industry with the aim of manipulating the AI systems themselves. One such emerging attack vector is indirect prompt injections. Unlike direct prompt injections, where an attacker directly inputs malicious commands into a prompt, indirect prompt injections involve hidden malicious instructions within external data sources. These may include emails, documents, or calendar invites that instruct AI to exfiltrate user data or execute other rogue actions. As more governments, businesses, and individuals adopt generative AI to get more done, this subtle yet potentially potent attack becomes increasingly pertinent across the industry, demanding immediate attention and robust security measures. At Google, our teams have a longstanding precedent of investing in a defense-in-depth strategy, including robust evaluation, threat analysis, AI security best practices , AI red-teaming , adversarial training, and model hardening for generative AI tools. This approach enables safer adoption of Gemini in Google Workspace and the Gemini app (we refer to both in this blog as “Gemini” for simplicity). Below we describe our prompt injection mitigation product strategy based on extensive research, development, and deployment of improved security mitigations. A layered security approach Google has taken a layered security approach introducing security measures designed for each stage of the prompt lifecycle. From Gemini 2.5 model hardening, to purpose-built machine learning (ML) models detecting malicious instructions, to system-level safeguards, we are meaningfully elevating the difficulty, expense, and complexity faced by an attacker. This approach compels adversaries to resort to methods that are either more easily identified or demand greater resources. findings.title: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite
findings.summary: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite Executive summary A group of Russian state-supported cyber actors has been targeting and compromising various Western government and commercial organizations using the Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) software since at least July 2025. The Russian state-supported advanced persistent threat (APT) group’s activity is tracked in the cybersecurity community under several names (see Cybersecurity industry tracking ), primarily as “LAUNDRY BEAR,” a name initially coined by the Netherlands General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) and Defence Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) [ 1 ]. LAUNDRY BEAR’s targeting is almost certainly to gather sensitive information for the Russian Federation, with these actors primarily focusing on the covert acquisition of email data. Previous campaigns indicated LAUNDRY BEAR relied on unsophisticated initial access techniques—including password spraying, phishing, and pass-the-cookie—allowing the group to successfully run high-volume operations. The latest campaign targeting ZCS uses a novel exploit that was a zero-day vulnerability when first exploited and continues to be successfully exploited. The vulnerability, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) CVE-2025-66376 , was patched in November 2025. This demonstrates LAUNDRY BEAR’s intent and ability to deploy increasingly sophisticated technical capabilities. Unlike traditional phishing campaigns that persuade a user into taking an action, such as clicking a link or opening a file, LAUNDRY BEAR’s latest campaign leverages a view-based exploit that only requires a user to view a malicious email within a vulnerable version of the webmail service. findings.title: Kubeflow Pipelines: Reflected XSS in the frontend pod information and events error responses
findings.summary:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines frontend reflected untrusted pod names and namespaces into HTML error responses from the pod-information and pod-events routes. An attacker could craft a link that causes JavaScript to execute in the frontend's origin when a user follows it and reaches an affected error response.

Affected routes include `/pipeline/k8s/pod` and `/pipeline/k8s/pod/events` (the deployment's configured base path may differ).

## Impact and prerequisites

Successful exploitation requires a victim to open an attacker-supplied link and reach the vulnerable response. JavaScript execution may expose information accessible to the victim's browser or perform actions in the application's origin.

The attacker does not need an account merely to construct and deliver the link. The victim must satisfy the deployment's authentication and route-access requirements. Cookie theft depends on cookie attributes and deployment protections; it is not guaranteed. The submitted evidence does not establish an availability impact or server-side code execution.

## Technical details

The pod handlers pass `podname` and `podnamespace` query values to `getPod` and `listPodEvents` in `frontend/server/k8s-helper.ts`. Before remediation, failure messages incorporated those values, along with backend error details, and were returned as HTML-capable string responses.

Kubernetes rejecting an invalid resource name did not prevent the issue: the rejected name could still be included in the frontend's error response.

[PR #12295](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/12295) changed the error construction to validate pod names and namespaces with `isAllowedResourceName`. Invalid values produce a constant error message instead of reflecting the supplied value, and backend error details are no longer included in these responses. The change includes invalid-resource-name tests.

## Affected versions and remediation

Affected product: the Kubeflow Pipelines frontend server, identified

findings.title: Kubeflow Pipelines: RBAC bypass on shared pipelines allows any authenticated user to delete or modify global pipelines
findings.summary:
## Summary

In multi-user mode, the Kubeflow Pipelines API server skipped authorization checks for shared/global pipelines with an empty namespace. This exception applied to write and delete operations as well as reads, allowing an authenticated user to modify or delete shared pipelines without the required Kubernetes RBAC permissions.

## Impact

Unauthorized modification compromises the integrity of shared pipeline definitions and versions. Unauthorized deletion can make shared pipelines unavailable.

Execution of a modified pipeline can cause attacker-controlled workload behavior, but this is a conditional downstream consequence requiring the modified pipeline to be executed. Modification alone does not demonstrate immediate worker code execution.

Reading shared pipelines is intentionally permitted and remains permitted after the fix. Consequently, access to shared pipeline configuration does not establish an additional confidentiality impact from this write-authorization defect. The confidentiality metric is None; the integrity and availability metrics reflect unauthorized modification and deletion of shared pipelines.

The affected authorization boundary is shared pipelines in multi-user deployments. Single-user deployments intentionally bypass these multi-user authorization checks.

## Patches

Fixed by [kubeflow/pipelines#13288](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/13288), with the fix included in 2.16.1.

Read-only operations on shared pipelines remain allowed. For write and delete operations, the API server checks Kubernetes RBAC permissions against the KFP system namespace, because shared pipelines have no namespace of their own.

## Scope of this fix

The 2.16.1 fix addresses the shared-pipeline authorization paths described above. It does not fix every shared-pipeline write path: the separate shared-pipeline upload authorization defect is tracked in [GHSA-rjr3-43j3-4q8g / CVE-2026-77596](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GH

findings.title: Kubeflow Pipelines — API server fetches a caller-supplied pipelineURL without host validation
findings.summary:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server fetched caller-supplied pipeline package URLs without restricting the destination. A caller authorized to create a pipeline or pipeline version could cause requests to originate from the API server's network position, including to internal services that the caller could not otherwise reach.

## Impact

The reported evidence demonstrates blind server-side request forgery and a limited status-code oracle. The fetched response is processed as a pipeline package; the report does not demonstrate arbitrary response-body disclosure or credential theft. A request to a cloud metadata endpoint returned HTTP 403, which does not establish access to metadata contents or tokens.

The confidentiality metric is Low to reflect the limited information obtainable through the status-code oracle. High confidentiality impact and integrity or availability impact are not established by the submitted evidence. Impact depends on the API server's network reachability and the deployment's trust boundaries.

## Patches

Fixed by [kubeflow/pipelines#12750](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/pull/12750), first released in 2.17.0. The fix validates URL schemes, ports, allowed domains, and resolved IP addresses; validates redirects; and enforces IP restrictions at connection time. The HTTP client also applies timeouts and disables environment proxy use so connections pass through the validated dialer.

Operators should keep pipeline URL validation enabled and limit additional allowed domains to trusted pipeline sources.

## Workarounds

Until upgrading, restrict API-server egress to required destinations through deployment-specific network controls. Account for required Kubernetes and storage connectivity when applying these restrictions.

## Related reports

This is the canonical advisory for the API-server pipeline URL SSRF family. [GHSA-wg4h-pp3x-hxhv](https://github.com/kubeflow/pipelines/security/advisories/GHSA-wg4h-pp3x-hxhv) is tracked as a d

findings.title: Kubeflow Pipelines: Cross-tenant execution-cache poisoning / output substitution via a namespace-blind cache key in the cache webhook (multi-user)
findings.summary:
## Summary

The legacy Kubeflow Pipelines V1/raw-Argo execution cache does not separate cached results by Kubernetes namespace. In multi-user deployments where tenants share the cache service, a tenant can receive another tenant's cached outputs or seed outputs that are subsequently substituted into another tenant's step.

This affects the Argo-template cache mutating webhook and its cache-server storage path. Standard KFP V2 component pods bypass this webhook cache; the separate V2 cache implementation is outside this advisory's scope.

## Affected deployments and impact

The issue requires multiple tenant namespaces sharing the legacy cache service, cache-enabled V1/raw-Argo steps, and cache entries that satisfy the configured staleness policy. The standard multi-user configuration watches pods across namespaces.

A tenant able to submit a step with the same cache-relevant template fields as another tenant's step can:

- Read cached step outputs originally produced in another namespace.
- Populate the shared cache before another tenant's matching step runs, causing that step to report the cached outputs instead of executing its intended containers.

Matching refers to the selected template fields used by the cache key, not merely an identical container image. This is an application-level cache-key collision caused by missing tenant scope, not a cryptographic SHA-256 collision. The finding establishes cross-namespace confidentiality and integrity impact; it does not establish arbitrary code execution.

## CVSS rationale

**Medium — CVSS 3.1: 5.4**

`CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N`

- **AV:N / PR:L / UI:N:** a tenant with ordinary workload-submission privileges can exercise the shared cache through network-accessible APIs. Reading an existing cached result or poisoning a subsequent automated execution requires no additional victim interaction.
- **AC:L:** known or shared templates can produce the same cache key deterministically. Cache-enabled executio

findings.title: FileGator: Missing authorization in GET /batchdownload allows cross-user retrieval of another user's archive
findings.summary:
### Summary
`GET /batchdownload` streams a batch ZIP to any requester who supplies its `uniqid`, without checking that the current user/session created it. In deployments where users have separate home directories, a valid low-privileged user who obtains an active archive id can download another user's batch archive, disclosing files the per-user boundary otherwise protects. Reported with explicit preconditions and bounded impact — not a universal "any user steals any file" issue.

### Details
The archive id is generated with plain `uniqid()` and no ownership metadata is bound to it before streaming.

- `backend/Services/Archiver/Adapters/ZipArchiver.php:44` — `createArchive()` uses plain `uniqid()`.
- `backend/Controllers/DownloadController.php:144-145` — `batchDownloadStart()` reads the tmpfs file by the request-supplied `uniqid` after only a charset `preg_replace()`.
- `backend/Controllers/DownloadController.php:158` — the tmpfs archive is removed only after streaming.
- `backend/Controllers/routes.php:207-226` — both batch endpoints are exposed to normal roles with `read`, `download`, `batchdownload`.

No user id, session id, home directory, or creator check is applied before streaming. The code path is unchanged since commit `3f03a40` (2022-05-31) and is present in the latest release `v7.14.3`.

### PoC
Preconditions: a multi-user deployment with distinct per-user `homedir`s (set per-user in `users.json`, or `private_repos => true` on the WordPress/LDAP adapter). The shipped sample config (`admin`/`guest` both at `/`, `guest` with no perms) does not create this boundary on its own. Attacker is a valid user with `read`, `download`, `batchdownload`.

2. User Jane (`homedir /jane`, with `batchdownload`) signs in normally.

findings.title: esm.sh: web.NewHandler allows arbitrary file read via encoded dot-segment path traversal
findings.summary:
### Summary

The documented `web.NewHandler` static file server can read files outside `Config.AppDir` when the request path contains URL-encoded dot-segments such as `%2e%2e`. Go's `ServeMux` redirects plain `/../` paths, but it passes encoded dot-segments to the handler after decoding `r.URL.Path`. The handler then calls `filepath.Join(s.config.AppDir, r.URL.Path)` without checking that the result remains under `AppDir`, allowing unauthenticated arbitrary file reads with the server process privileges.

### Details

`web/README.md:34-40` documents a network-facing setup:

```go
http.Handle("GET /", web.NewHandler(web.Config{
  AppDir: "/path/to/webapp",
  Fallback: "/index.html",
  Dev: false,
}))
log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
```

In `web/handler.go:62-75`, the handler takes `r.URL.Path` and joins it directly with `s.config.AppDir`:

```go
pathname := r.URL.Path
filename := filepath.Join(s.config.AppDir, pathname)
fi, err := os.Lstat(filename)
```

Later the same resolved filename is opened and copied to the response in `web/handler.go:150-166` for non-HTML/static files. There is no `filepath.IsLocal`, cleaned-relative-path, absolute-root prefix, or symlink-aware containment check before opening the file.

A plain `/../secret.txt` path is redirected by Go's `ServeMux`, but an encoded path such as `/%2e%2e/secret.txt` is decoded into `r.URL.Path == "/../secret.txt"` and reaches the handler. On Linux, `filepath.Join("/tmp/root/app", "/../secret.txt")` resolves to `/tmp/root/secret.txt`, outside the configured app directory.

Source-to-sink chain:

```text
Unauthenticated HTTP request path containing URL-encoded dot-segments
-> net/http decodes path into r.URL.Path
-> documented ServeMux setup passes encoded dot-segment path to web.NewHandler
-> web/handler.go joins Config.AppDir with r.URL.Path
-> os.Lstat/os.Open operate on the escaped path
-> io.Copy returns file contents to the attacker
```

False-positive checks performed:
- Plain dot-segment path

findings.title: fast-agent: `fast-agent serve` binds HTTP to 0.0.0.0 with no authentication by default; with --shell this is unauthenticated remote command execution
findings.summary:
## Summary
`fast-agent serve` exposes the agent over MCP. By default it uses HTTP transport bound to `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces) on port 8000 with **no authentication** (`auth=None`) and prints no warning. Any host that can reach the port can call the exposed `agent` tool. When the server is started with `--shell` (which is `-x`, the flag used in the README quickstart `uvx fast-agent mcp@latest -x`), the agent has a local `execute` shell tool, so an unauthenticated remote client can drive the agent into running arbitrary OS commands — unauthenticated RCE.

## Affected code
- `cli/commands/serve.py` — transport defaults to HTTP; `--host` defaults to `0.0.0.0`; port 8000.
- `mcp/server/agent_server.py` — `auth_provider = None` unless `FAST_AGENT_SERVE_OAUTH=huggingface`;
  `run_async(transport="http", host=host, ...)` with `host` defaulting to `0.0.0.0`.
- `tools/local_shell_executor.py` — the shell tool runs commands via `create_subprocess_shell`.

## Verified (live, faithful — published 0.7.20 in Docker python:3.13-slim, stock unauthenticated client)
1) Unauthenticated exposure (core defect): a client with no Authorization header completed
   `initialize` and `tools/list` (-> `['agent']`) against `http://HOST:8000/mcp`. Model-independent.
2) Unauthenticated RCE with `--shell`, demonstrated two ways:
   - Real production model (`gpt-4o-mini`): a single plain-language message asking the agent to run
     a command via its shell tool -> the model autonomously called `execute` and the command output
     (process identity showing it ran as root, the hostname, and the first lines of a sensitive
     system file) was returned to the unauthenticated caller.
   - Key-free deterministic (`passthrough` model): the tool-call directive invoked the shell tool
     directly, same result.
   The server-side permission prompt did not block this in non-interactive serve mode.

## Proof of concept
Environment: Docker `python:3.13-slim`, `pip install fast-agent-mcp` -> 0.7.20.

```

traQ: Privilege escalation by OAuth prompt=none request
findings.summary:
In OAuth2 silent authorization (`prompt=none`), when the `scope` parameter was empty or omitted, all scopes registered for the OAuth client became eligible for issuance. However, the prior consent check was performed against the empty requested scope set. As a result, an attacker could obtain an access token with broader scopes than the user had previously consented to, without requiring additional consent.

## Impact

If an attacker controls an OAuth client capable of receiving authorization codes, and a user has already consented to only a subset of that client’s scopes, the attacker may be able to obtain a token containing all scopes registered for that client by sending an authorization request with `prompt=none` and an empty or omitted `scope`.

If the user has not consented to the client at all, `consent_required` is returned as usual.

## Patches

This issue has been fixed in v3.28.3. After the fix, the consent check for `prompt=none` verifies the scopes that will actually be issued, rather than the empty requested scope set. If the user has not consented to all scopes after expansion, `consent_required` is returned.

traQ also recommends revoking any existing OAuth tokens created before the fix if they were potentially affected.

## Workarounds

If users cannot update immediately, they should apply the following mitigations:

- Disable untrusted OAuth clients, minimize registered client scopes, and revoke existing tokens
- Reject authorization requests with `prompt=none` where `scope` is empty or omitted

findings.title: isomorphic-git: Path traversal via a ".." tree-entry name writes files outside the working directory on clone/checkout
findings.summary:
### Summary
isomorphic-git's tree parser (`src/models/GitTree.js`) validates each entry name only against the path separators `/` and `\`. It does not reject the standalone reserved name `..`, so a malicious repository can, on a single `clone`/`checkout`, **write files outside the working
directory** (unbounded depth). Works on any host-backed `fs` provider.

### Details
The guard is:

```js
// src/models/GitTree.js
if (path.includes('\\') || path.includes('/')) {
  throw new UnsafeFilepathError(path)
}
```

The standalone string `..` passes. isomorphic-git assembles the full path incrementally across tree levels, so nesting `..` trees yields `../escaped.txt`, `../../escaped.txt`, … with unbounded depth (each level is a separate tree object that passes the per-entry guard). On checkout `mkdir(workdir/..)` hits `EEXIST` (ignored) and the file is written above the working directory. Depth is chosen to reach the home dir, `/etc`, `/tmp`, etc.; overwriting a shell rc / config / startup file can escalate to code execution.

#### Canonical git behavior (divergence)
git rejects this via `verify_path()`: `git read-tree` fails with `error: invalid path '../escaped.txt'` and `git fsck` flags `warning … hasDotdot: contains '..'`. (git's `verify_path` also rejects `.` and `.git`, the latter flagged by fsck as `hasDotgit` — see the fix note below.) GitHub runs fsck on push, so such a tree can't be hosted there; reach is limited to a self-hosted/Smart-HTTP remote or a MitM.


### PoC
`https://github.com/spiceoverflow/av2-dotdot-traversal` — open in a Codespace; a single `git.clone()` from the bundled server writes `escaped.txt` one directory above the clone target (`DEPTH=N` escapes N levels):

```
[AV-2] *** PATH TRAVERSAL CONFIRMED ***
[AV-2] File written outside workdir: …/escaped.txt
```

### Impact
A path-traversal arbitrary file write outside the working directory (CWE-22), triggered by a single clone/checkout; it can escalate to code execution by overwriting shell rc, conf

findings.title: fastapi-code-generator: Import-time RCE via route path -> unescaped @app.get('...') decorator
findings.summary:
### Summary

fastapi-code-generator (koxudaxi) emits the OpenAPI path into the generated main.py route decorator as a single-quoted string literal (`@app.get('/u/<path>/x')`) without escaping the `'`. A `'` in the path closes the decorator string and, via concatenation, injects a live expression that the decorator argument evaluates when main.py is imported (the ASGI server imports it at startup) -- code execution, no request needed. The path is a pure data field. Verified on fastapi-code-generator 0.8.0 / Python 3 / FastAPI.

### Details

```python
@app.get('/u/'+(__import__("os").system('…') or "")+'/x', response_model=None)
def get_thing() -> None:
 pass
```

The generator post-processes output with black/isort, so a syntax-breaking payload aborts generation (DoS); a valid-Python concat (`'+expr+'`, kept valid with `(… or "")`) is written and runs at import. info.description (`description='…'`), tags, and parameter defaults are `'`-escaped; the path in @app.get('…') is the unescaped sink. Models come from datamodel-code-generator (repr-escaped, no RCE).

Not a duplicate: distinct product from OpenAPI Generator's python-fastapi backend (different codebase/template/decorator); and distinct from the operation-summary docstring sink in the same product.

### PoC

`reproduce.sh` (+ `make_spec.py`) attached: generates the app and merely imports main.py; the injected expression runs at decorator evaluation and writes a marker. Verified on 0.8.0.

### Impact

Code execution at import/startup in any application/CI that generates a FastAPI app with fastapi-code-generator from an attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced spec and imports/serves it. Estimated Critical, e.g. `CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`.

### Suggested fix

Escape the path for the Python string literal (escape ', \, newlines via repr) before emitting @app.get('…'), and validate path characters.

findings.title: Bringing Rust to the Pixel Baseband
findings.summary: Posted by Jiacheng Lu, Software Engineer, Google Pixel Team Google is continuously advancing the security of Pixel devices. We have been focusing on hardening the cellular baseband modem against exploitation. Recognizing the risks associated within the complex modem firmware, Pixel 9 shipped with mitigations against a range of memory-safety vulnerabilities. For Pixel 10, Google is advancing its proactive security measures further. Following our previous discussion on "Deploying Rust in Existing Firmware Codebases" , this post shares a concrete application: integrating a memory-safe Rust DNS(Domain Name System) parser into the modem firmware. The new Rust-based DNS parser significantly reduces our security risk by mitigating an entire class of vulnerabilities in a risky area, while also laying the foundation for broader adoption of memory-safe code in other areas. Here we share our experience of working on it, and hope it can inspire the use of more memory safe languages in low-level environments. Why Modem Memory Safety Can’t Wait In recent years, we have seen increasing interest in the cellular modem from attackers and security researchers. For example, Google's Project Zero gained remote code execution on Pixel modems over the Internet. Pixel modem has tens of Megabytes of executable code. Given the complexity and remote attack surface of the modem, other critical memory safety vulnerabilities may remain in the predominantly memory-unsafe firmware code. Why DNS? The DNS protocol is most commonly known in the context of browsers finding websites. With the evolution of cellular technology, modern cellular communications have migrated to digital data networks; consequently, even basic operations such as call forwarding rely on DNS services. DNS is a complex protocol and requires parsing of untrusted data, which can lead to vulnerabilities, particularly when implemented in a memory-unsafe language (example: CVE-2024-27227 ). Implementing the DNS parser in Rust offers
